description: We are ASTABLES group, an Electronic Engineering team from La Paz, Bolivia. Our name comes from astable multivibrators, electronic circuits that continuously oscillate between states without ever remaining in a stable state. This principle reflects our philosophy: never standing still, constantly innovating, and transforming scientific data into technological solutions to address real-world challenges facing our planet
summary: AYNOKA is a decision-support prototype for crop rotation in the Bolivian Altiplano, developed by the ASTABLES team at UMSA. It combines historical NASA POWER climate data for Patacamaya and Viacha with an explainable engine that compares three crop rotation strategies according to users’ priorities: water conservation, soil recovery, and production. The project also includes a hardware prototype concept for soil analysis and monitoring, represented in the application through simulated sensor readings and a data collection workflow. Its interactive interface presents climate indicators, three-year rotation plans, and explanations of the results. AYNOKA brings climate information, soil-monitoring concepts, and agricultural planning together to help farmers and technical advisers explore locally relevant alternatives. The public demonstration implements the software workflow, while physical hardware integration and field validation remain the next development steps.
details:
AYNOKA is an agricultural decision-support prototype developed by the ASTABLES team at Universidad Mayor de San Andrés (UMSA). It combines historical climate information, crop rotation strategies, and a hardware prototype concept for soil analysis and monitoring. The demonstration focuses on Patacamaya and Viacha in the Bolivian Altiplano.

The project integrates daily NASA POWER meteorological data from 2020 through 2025, with MERRA-2 identified as an underlying source. It uses corrected precipitation, mean temperature, minimum temperature, maximum temperature, and relative humidity. These records are processed into agricultural seasons running from September through April, producing indicators such as accumulated rainfall, average temperature, absolute minimum temperature, and days with minimum temperatures below freezing.

AYNOKA compares three predefined, three-year crop rotation strategies. Users select their priorities for water conservation, soil recovery, and production. A weighted multicriteria evaluation engine combines those preferences with climate inputs to rank the alternatives. The interface displays each criterion’s contribution and explains the resulting recommendation, allowing users to explore how different priorities influence their rotation plans.

A central component of the proposal is a hardware prototype for soil analysis and monitoring, organized around field sensor nodes and a central collection station. The software demonstration represents this architecture through simulated readings, configurable sensor values, data packets, and monitoring alerts. Soil-moisture readings illustrate how local observations could complement regional climate information and help characterize conditions relevant to crop planning.

The monitoring workflow also incorporates an experimental continuous-learning module built with River. It processes simulated soil-moisture readings and identifies unusual patterns over time. The public demonstration implements the software side of this workflow; connecting physical instruments, calibrating sensors, and testing the complete prototype in agricultural plots are the next development steps.

AYNOKA is implemented using Python, Streamlit, pandas, and Plotly. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js support its interactive interface and three-dimensional visual environment. The application connects climate exploration, priority selection, rotation comparison, and simulated soil monitoring within a single demonstration.

The project’s creative contribution is its combination of NASA climate data, explainable agricultural planning, and a soil-monitoring hardware concept adapted to the Altiplano context. Its intended impact is to make technical information easier to understand, support collaboration between farmers and agricultural advisers, and provide a foundation for evaluating crop rotation alternatives under local water, soil, and temperature conditions.
